At 4:17 every morning, the lighthouse blinked at a town that no longer existed.

The town had slid into the sea years ago, house by house, street by street, until only the church bell remained above water. On calm days, fishermen could see it shining green beneath the waves. On stormy days, they could hear it ring.

Mara kept the lighthouse. She had inherited it from her father, who had inherited it from his mother, who had come to the coast with a suitcase and a story she refused to tell. The light still turned, though no ships used this stretch of coast anymore. The harbor had silted up. The road had washed away. The mapmakers had stopped drawing the lighthouse.

Still, each night, Mara climbed the spiral stairs and polished the lens.

At 4:17, the lamp blinked once toward the water.

Then, one winter morning, it blinked twice.

Mara looked up from her coffee. The light had never blinked twice.

Outside, the sea lay smooth as dark glass. She took her father’s brass spyglass from its hook and aimed it toward the place where the town had been.

A figure stood on the surface of the water.

It wore a yellow coat. It was much too small to be a shipwrecked sailor, and much too still to be a bird.

Mara lowered the spyglass.

When she looked again, the figure was closer.

She ran down the lighthouse stairs, pulling on her boots as she went. By the time she reached the shore, the tide had turned. The figure was a child, ankle-deep in the water, holding a red tin pail.

“Are you lost?” Mara called.

The child looked up. “No,” she said. “I’m waiting for my mother.”

Mara knew then—not from the child’s face, but from the shape of her voice. It was the voice in the old stories, the one her grandmother had used when talking about the town beneath the sea.

“What’s your name?” Mara asked.

“Lena.”

The child’s name was written in the church register, in a book Mara had found beneath the lighthouse floorboards. Lena Vale. Age seven. Missing, though no one had written down when she disappeared.

“Your mother isn’t here,” Mara said carefully.

“She said she’d come back when the light blinked twice.”

Mara glanced at the lighthouse. From the shore, its lamp appeared steady and white.

“I’m afraid you’ve been waiting a long time.”

Lena shrugged. “I’m good at waiting.”

The child turned toward the water. Far out, beneath the glassy surface, a bell gave one slow, green flash.

Mara took off her coat and wrapped it around Lena’s shoulders. It smelled of salt, old wool, and coffee. Then she held out her hand.

“Come inside,” she said. “We’ll wait together.”

Lena studied her. “Will you keep the light on?”

“Yes.”

“Even when no one can see it?”

Mara thought of the vanished roads, the empty harbor, the maps that had forgotten them.

“Especially then,” she said.

Together they climbed the stairs. At the top, the lamp turned toward the sea. It swept once across the empty horizon, then returned, patient as a heartbeat.

At 4:17 the next morning, the bell rang.

And, somewhere beneath the water, a window lit up.
